--- title: "The Normal Distribution, Interactively" description: "Move the sliders, hover the charts and rotate the surface to build real intuition for the most important distribution in statistics." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-09-27 categories: [Statistics, Distributions] --- The normal distribution appears everywhere: measurement error, heights, test scores and the sampling distribution of almost any average. Instead of memorising its formula, let us **play with it**. ::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will learn - How $\mu$ and $\sigma$ shape the bell curve - Where the 68–95–99.7 rule comes from - How two correlated normals form a 3D surface ::: ## The formula A random variable $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has density $$ f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) $$ {#eq-normal} ## Explore the parameters Drag the sliders. The shaded band is $\mu \pm k\sigma$, and the readout shows the probability it contains. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js" viewof mu = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean μ"}) viewof sigma = Inputs.range([0.6, 2.5], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Std dev σ"}) viewof k = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.5, label: "Band ±kσ"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false pdf = x => Math.exp(-((x - mu) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2)) / (sigma * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)) erf = x => { const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * Math.abs(x)); const y = 1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x); return x >= 0 ? y : -y; } prob = erf(k / Math.SQRT2) curve = d3.range(-7, 7.01, 0.02).map(x => ({x, y: pdf(x)})) band = curve.filter(d => d.x >= mu - k * sigma && d.x <= mu + k * sigma) html`
P(μ − ${k}σ ≤ X ≤ μ + ${k}σ)${(prob * 100).toFixed(1)}%
` ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ ...msStyle, x: {domain: [-7, 7], label: "x"}, y: {domain: [0, 0.7], label: "Density"}, marks: [ Plot.areaY(band, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: ms.indigo, fillOpacity: 0.18}), Plot.line(curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeWidth: 2.5}), Plot.ruleX([mu], {stroke: ms.indigo, strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeOpacity: 0.7}), Plot.ruleY([0], {strokeOpacity: 0.25}), Plot.tip(curve, Plot.pointerX({x: "x", y: "y", title: d => `x = ${d.x.toFixed(2)}\nf(x) = ${d.y.toFixed(3)}`})) ] }) ``` ::: {.callout-note} ## The 68–95–99.7 rule Set the band to $1\sigma$, $2\sigma$ and $3\sigma$. The readout gives about 68.3%, 95.4% and 99.7%, no matter what $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are. ::: ## Samples versus theory Hover over the bars to read exact values. Drag to zoom and double-click to reset. ::: {#cell-fig-hist .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from scipy import stats from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG # also registers the "mlstation" Plotly theme rng = np.random.default_rng(0) samples = rng.normal(0, 1, 10_000) x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_histogram(x=samples, histnorm="probability density", nbinsx=70, name="Samples", marker=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], opacity=0.35, line=dict(width=0))) fig.add_scatter(x=x, y=stats.norm.pdf(x), mode="lines", name="Theory", line=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], width=3)) fig.update_layout(height=360, xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="Density", bargap=0.02, hovermode="x unified") fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG) ``` ::: {#fig-hist .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` 10,000 draws from a standard normal, with the theoretical density overlaid. ::: ::: ## Two variables at once With correlation $\rho$, two normals form a bivariate surface. **Rotate it** by dragging. $$ f(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2 - 2\rho xy + y^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right) $$ ::: {#cell-fig-surface .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from ms_charts import SURFACE_SCALE, PLOTLY_CONFIG rho = 0.6 g = np.linspace(-3, 3, 80) X, Y = np.meshgrid(g, g) Z = np.exp(-(X**2 - 2*rho*X*Y + Y**2) / (2*(1 - rho**2))) / (2*np.pi*np.sqrt(1 - rho**2)) fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x=X, y=Y, z=Z, colorscale=SURFACE_SCALE, showscale=False, contours=dict(z=dict(show=True, usecolormap=True, project_z=True)))) fig.update_layout(height=420, margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=0, b=0), scene=dict(xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="y", zaxis_title="density", camera=dict(eye=dict(x=1.5, y=1.3, z=0.75)), aspectratio=dict(x=1, y=1, z=0.6), xaxis=dict(backgroundcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), yaxis=dict(backgroundcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), zaxis=dict(backgroundcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)"))) fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG) ``` ::: {#fig-surface .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Bivariate normal density with correlation ρ = 0.6. ::: ::: ## Checking normality A Q–Q plot compares sample quantiles with theoretical ones. Points on the line mean the data is close to normal. This chart is a static image, drawn with the shared MLStation style. ::: {#cell-fig-qq .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy import stats from ms_charts import style_matplotlib, COLORS style_matplotlib() rng = np.random.default_rng(3) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.4), sharey=False) for ax, data, title, c in [(axes[0], rng.normal(size=300), "Normal sample", COLORS["indigo"]), (axes[1], rng.exponential(size=300), "Skewed sample", COLORS["rose"])]: (osm, osr), (slope, icpt, _) = stats.probplot(data) ax.scatter(osm, osr, s=10, color=c, alpha=.7, linewidths=0) ax.plot(osm, slope * osm + icpt, color="#8A93A3", lw=1.2, ls="--") ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("Theoretical quantiles") axes[0].set_ylabel("Sample quantiles") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Normal data follows the line; skewed data bends away from it.](normal-distribution-interactive_files/figure-html/fig-qq-output-1.png){#fig-qq width=866 height=361} ::: ::: ## Summary - $\mu$ shifts the curve, $\sigma$ stretches it, and the area always equals 1. - About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values fall within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. - Use Q–Q plots, not just histograms, to check normality.
